title: Task: a promise of a result
sub: A claim ticket instead of the answer
cards/0/title: A Task is a claim ticket
cards/0/body:
A Task is an object meaning "work that will finish later". Think of a dry cleaner's ticket: your clothes aren't ready yet, but you hold a slip you'll trade for them later.

A Task<string> is a ticket you'll trade for a string.
cards/1/body:
There are two ways to collect the result.

await t: if the task isn't done yet, the method releases the thread and resumes when the result appears (that's the continuation from the previous lesson).

t.Result: the thread stands and waits, like the waiter by the stove. On the UI thread that is the same freeze as a synchronous call, and sometimes a permanent one (we'll get to that in u4).

A task ends in one of three ways: success (with a result), an error (the Faulted state), or cancellation (Canceled). Until then it is in progress.
cards/1/code:
Task<string> t = http.GetStringAsync(url); // request sent, ticket in hand
DoOtherWork();                              // free to do something else
string html = await t;                      // thread is free while we wait
// string html = t.Result;                  // thread stands still while we wait
cards/1/deep: TaskStatus: Created, WaitingForActivation, WaitingToRun, Running, WaitingForChildrenToComplete, RanToCompletion, Canceled, Faulted. Tasks from async methods and I/O are usually WaitingForActivation: they aren't "running" on any thread, and something outside will complete them.
cards/2/pairs/1/1: The same, with an int result
cards/3/q: A method returned Task<string>. Where is the string?
cards/3/options/0: It may not exist yet: await hands it over when the task completes
cards/3/explain: A task is a promise. The result appears when the operation finishes.
cards/4/q: How can a task end? Select all that apply.
cards/4/explain: Those are the three final states. You can't pause a task.
cards/5/body:
Creating a thread for every small piece of work is expensive: each thread has its own stack (on the order of a megabyte), and the OS spends time creating it and switching between threads.

So .NET has a thread pool: a few pre-created background threads and a shared work queue. Right away the pool is ready to give you roughly as many threads as the CPU has cores.

Task.Run(f) puts f into the pool's queue and immediately returns a Task. A free pool thread takes the work and runs it; when f finishes, the task completes.

If all threads are busy, the work waits in the queue. The pool will add a thread eventually, but not right away. Remember this: in u4.l5 it becomes a problem.
cards/5/flow/2: a free pool thread runs f
cards/6/body:
Heavy computation inside a handler occupies the UI thread, and the window freezes. Task.Run moves it to the pool. Step by step:

1. The UI thread writes "Compressing…".
2. Task.Run puts Compress into the pool's queue and returns an incomplete task.
3. await sees the task isn't done, and the handler returns control: the window responds to clicks.
4. A pool thread finishes compressing, and the task completes.
5. The rest of the handler is put into the UI thread's queue and runs there, so it may touch Status.

Why await in a window comes back to the UI thread specifically is covered in detail in u4.l1. I/O doesn't need Task.Run: GetStringAsync already doesn't hold a thread.
cards/6/deep: Task.Run(async () => …) unwraps the inner task correctly. Task.Factory.StartNew with an async lambda returns Task<Task>: the outer task completes as soon as the lambda reaches its first real pause and returns the inner task. await waits only for that, not for the whole job. A classic mistake.
cards/7/q: You need to compress a large image without freezing the window. What do you do?
cards/7/options/1: Call Compress(img) directly in the handler
cards/7/explain: Compress is CPU work. Calling it directly in the handler occupies the UI thread, and the window stops responding. Task.Run moves the work to the pool, and the handler releases the UI thread at await. After compression, the rest runs on the UI thread again.
cards/7/wrong/1: Compression takes over the UI thread: the message loop stops until Compress finishes.
cards/7/wrong/2: The pool does the compressing, but the UI thread stands on .Result until it's done, so the window freezes just the same.
cards/8/q: Should you wrap http.GetStringAsync(url) in Task.Run?
cards/8/options/0: No: the request doesn't hold a thread anyway; Task.Run only adds a hop to the pool
cards/8/options/1: Yes, or it will block the window
cards/8/explain: GetStringAsync sends the request and returns a task right away; no thread waits on the network. Task.Run only adds a trip through the pool's queue and back.
cards/8/deep: The exception is "async" APIs that do noticeable synchronous work before their first real pause: for example, the old HttpWebRequest in .NET Framework could resolve DNS and detect proxies synchronously, and some database drivers behave similarly. For those, Task.Run in a UI app is sometimes justified, but only profiling tells you so.
cards/9/q: Get the result without blocking the thread
cards/9/explain: await "unwraps" a Task<string> into a string.
